title: The Dizzy Spinner
briefing: Amara, 13, spins around ten times on a playground spinner. When it stops, the playground seems to keep turning, she wobbles, and her friend sees her eyes flicking side to side. About half a minute later it's all gone.
question: Why does the world keep spinning after Amara has stopped?

clues.title: Still turning
clues.text: When the spinner stops, the playground seems to keep turning the other way. Closing her eyes doesn't stop the feeling.
clues.shows: her balance sense reporting a spin that isn't happening, even with her eyes shut

clues.title: Wobbly steps
clues.text: She stumbles sideways when she tries to walk and grabs the rail. Her legs feel shaky.

clues.title: Flicking eyes
clues.text: For a few seconds after she stops, her friend sees Amara's eyes flicking quickly side to side. Amara isn't doing it on purpose.
clues.shows: the eyes trying to follow a spin the inner ear says is still happening

clues.title: More spins, longer
clues.text: After 5 spins the dizziness lasts a few seconds; after 20 spins it lasts about half a minute. Then it fades completely.
clues.shows: the effect growing with how much she spun and fading by itself

hypotheses.text: Her blood sugar is low because she skipped a snack.
hypotheses.flaw: Low fuel doesn't arrive the moment a spinner stops and vanish thirty seconds later — and it wouldn't make the playground seem to turn.

hypotheses.text: Fluid in the balance loops of her inner ear started swirling while she spun; when she stopped, it kept swirling for a while, so her brain was told she was still turning.
She bumped her head on the spinner.
hypotheses.flaw: Nothing hit her head, and the dizziness grew with the number of spins and was gone in half a minute.

hypotheses.text: Her eyes are tired from watching the world go by.
hypotheses.flaw: She still felt she was turning with her eyes closed, so the feeling isn't coming from her eyes.

prediction.prompt: Amara spins more and more times — from none up to twenty. Right after she stops, how dizzy does she feel?

second.question: And as the seconds pass after she stops, what happens to the dizziness?

concepts.label: the inner ear
concepts.hint: Where in the body is your balance sense?

concepts.label: fluid swirls
concepts.hint: What is inside those balance loops, and what does spinning do to it?

concepts.label: keeps going after stopping
concepts.hint: Why doesn't it stop when the spinner does?

concepts.label: the brain is fooled
concepts.hint: Who is being told she's still turning?

concepts.label: it settles by itself
concepts.hint: What happened after half a minute?

transfer.context: After a long ride on the spinning teacups at a fair, Ravi steps off and the ground seems to tilt and turn. He has to sit down for a minute until it passes.
options: His shoes are slippery on the grass.
The fluid in his inner ear kept swirling after the ride stopped, telling his brain he was still turning.
He was scared of the ride.
The music at the fair was too loud.
transfer.retryHint: The world keeps turning after the spinning stops — which of Amara's clues was exactly that?
transfer.explanation: The teacups set the fluid in Ravi's inner-ear loops swirling. When the ride stopped, the fluid didn't — so for a minute his brain was still being told he was turning, just like Amara on the playground.

takeaway: Your balance sense lives in fluid-filled loops in your inner ear. Spinning sets the fluid swirling, and because it keeps going after you stop, your brain thinks you are still turning until it settles.
